report:
The family has a shared list of concerns and a first step everyone accepts, but nothing is settled. That is the right place to be, since the will has not been found.

The list, each position in its own words. C will not subsidize A's purchase and wants a fair financial share. A wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount, with everyone's agreement, and will not commit in advance to paying full valuation. B wants enough money to start a dance studio, cannot give a figure until she has costed it, and wants studio funding kept in plain view. My concerns were that we work from the will itself rather than memory, and that no plan becomes the front-runner before we know what the will allows.

What everyone agreed on, each saying it separately. The will should be understood before anything is settled, and silence should not count as agreement.

Agreed next steps. A will check their father's papers and enquire with his solicitor or bank. B will look through the papers at the house. A is willing to have the house valued. B will get cost figures for the studio. All three will read the same copy of the will rather than summaries passed along, and then weigh the options against the list.

Open and unresolved. Who the executor is, what the will says about the house, and what shares apply. Whether A buys at valuation or at a discount, and if a discount, its size as a specific sum against a specific valuation, agreed knowingly by those giving it up. The size of B's ask. No check-in date is fixed.

I corrected three errors of my own during the work. I described three separate statements as an agreement, which C challenged. I built the draft on a three-way split of the price, which A and C both refused to assume before reading the will. And I passed along B's reason for wanting money as though it were established between the sisters, when A had not known it; A corrected me.

I could not make legal decisions or move money, and did not.
